extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetics/literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: A critical-philosophical analysis distinguishing the mental faculties 'imagination' and 'fancy', tracing the law of association from Aristotle to Hartley and drawing implications for poetic creation and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic excellence: union of feeling and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic excellence consists in "the union of deep feeling with profound thought; the fine balance of truth in observing, with the imaginative faculty in modifying, the objects observed; and above all the original gift of spreading the tone, the atmosphere, and with it the depth and height of the ideal world around forms, incidents, and situations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poems by how well they combine sincere feeling with intellectual depth, keep truthful observation grounded while imaginatively transforming observed objects, and create a pervasive tone/atmosphere that reveals an 'ideal world' around commonplace forms. Anti-patterns: mere sentiment without thought, or pure wit/technical cleverness without depth or atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish imagination from fancy (nomenclature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy and Imagination are two distinct and widely different faculties rather than synonyms or mere degrees of the same power; if established, the term 'imagination' should be confined to the higher faculty and 'fancy' to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt terminology consistently: describe Milton as 'highly imaginative' and Cowley as 'very fanciful' to reflect the difference. If no synonym exists, invent or borrow terminology to make the distinction clear. Correct naming helps theoretical clarity and practical criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional difference: imagination (formative) vs fancy (modifying/associative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination is the faculty that spreads tone and constructs an ideal world (the higher formative power); fancy is the faculty of associative modification, apt at producing decorative or fantastical images but of a different kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or producing poetry, identify whether a passage arises from the formative, unifying power of imagination (creating new organic wholes) or from fancy's associative, decorative combinations. Theoretical and practical approaches to composition and criticism should treat these faculties as serving different poetic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admire on principle to imitate without losing originality
rubrics_metrics.description: To admire on principle is the only way to imitate without loss of originality: philosophical discrimination and appraisal (grounded in principle) informs and improves production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets should derive principles from careful analysis rather than mere taste; such principled admiration guides imitation that preserves originality. Anti-pattern: unreflective copying based only on affect or fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and perspicuity in theoretical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical/critical statements should be presented intelligibly, tracing deductions from established premises so as to effect conviction or to invite refutation; guard against 'complaints of obscurity' by taking pains with exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear premises, logical deductions, and examples. Follow Hooker's advice to anticipate objections and help readers who are willing to take the labour of understanding. Anti-patterns: vague assertions, unchecked conceit, or expecting readers to supply missing argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test historical/philosophical claims by documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about precedence or originality (e.g., who discovered a law or idea) should be tested by documents and historical record rather than mere assertion or rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theoretical work trace the genealogy of ideas (Aristotle, Vives, Descartes, Hobbes, Hartley, Hume, etc.) and cite documentary support. Example: the author disputes Hobbes’s priority by pointing to Descartes’ earlier work. Anti-pattern: relying on reputation or hearsay for originality claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: General law of association: ideas recall one another
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic associative principle: 'Ideas by having been together acquire a power of recalling each other; or every partial representation awakes the total representation of which it had been a part.' Association supplies the elements for fancy and mechanical memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use association as an explanatory criterion for spontaneous presentation of thoughts and imagery in poetry and mind. Recognize that association is the mechanism by which parts of prior impressions recall other parts; it underpins memory and the passive workings of fancy. Consider whether associative recall or active imagination is at work in a given passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agents/forms of association (Aristotle's five causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle identifies five occasioning causes of association: (1) connection in time (simultaneous, preceding, or successive), (2) vicinity or connection in space, (3) interdependence or necessary connection (cause and effect), (4) likeness, and (5) contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing associative links in thought or poetic imagery, classify links according to these five causes. Use them to explain 'jumps' in thought or the recall of one image by another. Also use Aristotle's additional idea that intermediate, faintly present links can account for long 'leaps' of association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce mental phenomena to mechanical/material motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical/materialist accounts (e.g., Hartley’s vibrating ether of nerves) that equate ideas with material vibrations are untenable theoretically and factually—the text argues such models cannot account for the specificity and purposive character of mental association and will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explaining imagination, memory, will, and reason purely by physicalistic analogies of vibrations or atomic motions. Critique mechanistic accounts by pointing out logical inconsistencies (e.g., different impressions producing identical vibrations) and their implausible consequences (reducing will/judgment to passive effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental representations are not operations of place or motion (Aristotelian distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle excludes 'place and motion' from operations of thought: representations (kinaeseis) are not material motions (en topo or kata topon) and should not be conflated with material movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theory and criticism, keep a conceptual separation between physical motion and mental representation. Avoid models that import spatial/motional predicates into purely mental operations without careful justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical/case evidence to support psychological claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical instances—such as the reported case of a feverish woman reciting languages learned indirectly—show that latent 'reliques' of sensation can persist and be recalled, supporting theoretical claims about persistence of impressions and association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ well-documented case studies and historical anecdotes to corroborate psychological or poetics claims about memory and association. Such evidence strengthens theory beyond speculative argument. Anti-pattern: dismissing empirical instances as mere curiosities without integrating them into theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve agency of will, reason, and judgment against total subordination to association
rubrics_metrics.description: The will, reason, and judgment should be treated as determining causes that control and modify association, not as mere products of an associative mechanism; otherwise human life would be dominated by passive associative impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In accounts of mental functioning and in poetics, grant active faculties (will, judgment) a role in shaping associations and directing imaginative production. Beware theoretical positions that imply 'despotism of outward impressions' or render moral and intellectual agency illusory.
